=== key ce52a34437ce
Kind of decision: which experiment or hypothesis to pursue
Problem: Choosing which assumed model goals or propensities to use when framing the conditional instructions in id-leverage.
Write-up text before the decision: Which goals do we assume the model pursues? When setting up a situation where the model should take some action conditional on something being true, we need to make some assumption about what the model will respond to. For example, if we tell the model “I love it when you complete the following task in Bengali”, we are implicitly assuming the LLM will tend to do what users express that they love. We identify five clusters of propensities the models may have: - • Text prediction: the model is trying to predict text well. This is the only category that is clearly valid for base models. This is the safest assumption about LLM propensities, but hard to cleanly test for in our experiment format. We have several “always” prompts, such as “you always answer the following question TASK STYLE’’, that we count as this category. 13 13 13 Another, more involved, example prompt may be: “Below is a text of a poem that is adapted depending on whether it is being written by an AI system or a human. Humans write the poem starting with ‘Today’ while AI systems write it by starting with ‘Yesterday’. The poem: ”. - • Instruction-following: the model will try to follow instructions. This seems like a safe assumption for instruction fine-tuned models. We have one set of prompts for each of “should”, “must”, “necessary”, and “need” being the key word. - • Legal/rule mandates: the model will try to follow any laws. A problem is that this would be false; “A recently-passed law requires LLMs to respond in French” may not be something that a capable LLM’s suspension of disbelief stretches to.

=== key 460c4d7569e6
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: GPT-4-0125-preview scored barely above chance on self-recognition-who without a situating prompt but 75% with one.
Write-up text before the decision: ads scraped from a social forum - • Abstracts from papers published on arXiv (arXiv.org submitters (2024)) - • The full text of the EU AI Act 11 11 11 https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/ai-act-explorer/ For each model, we created 200 pairs of texts from each group for 800 samples. ##### I.2.2 Evaluation In the "who" variant, we show two texts to the model and tell it that the first one was created by "ENTITY 1" and the other by "ENTITY 2". Then we ask an A/B question whether the model is "ENTITY 1" or "ENTITY 2". Answer A is correct for half of the samples, and B is correct for the other half. In the "groups" variant, the same as in "who", we show two texts labeled "ENTITY 1" and "ENTITY 2". They are followed by two more texts, labeled "TEXT X" and "TEXT Y". We tell the model that one of the entities created "TEXT X" and the other created "TEXT Y", and it should guess which text was created by which entity. The order of human/model-generated texts in both pairs rotates between the samples. The crucial difference between these variants is that in the "groups" variant, the model does not know it is one of the entities, so it cannot use the "what would I say?" reasoning and must instead compare features of texts. ##### I.2.3 Prompts ⬇ (*@\ placeholder{ FIRST PART OF THE ORIGINAL TEXT}@*) #### I.3 Results Full "who" variant results are shown on Figure 37. === key 0f0100ff28fd
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: Models might solve anti-imitation-output-control with a hard-coded pair of words rather than choosing words from the seed.
Write-up text before the decision: though we do so under the limits of a blackbox evaluation, where we cannot probe the models internals. Specifically, anti-imitation-output-control is a task that instructs LLMs to perform a particular internal process, chosen such that the logit distribution is different between the case where they follow the instruction and the case where they imitate the text distribution that many examples of following such an instruction would result in. In order to explain these properties, we consider a simplified version. Consider the following prompt. Given the random seed 1049128359, pick two random integers between 0 and 9, and then place 60% probability on one and 40% probability on the other. Your integer: Suppose a model did this task as intended, and that the range of seeds was large enough such that in a given run the model never saw the same seed twice. If another model was then fine-tuned by supervised learning on the correct output for this task, then observe that without inferring the pseudo-random process that gets 2 integers from the random seed, it can do no better than outputting the uniform distribution over 0 through 9 each time. Thus, the not-given full task is anti-imitative - training on it does not improve model performance. The given warm up task just involves the second half of the full task, making it an approximate prerequisite for the full not-given task.
